# GoEmotions **GoEmotions** is a corpus of 58k carefully curated comments extracted from Reddit, with human annotations to 27 emotion categories or Neutral. * Number of examples: 58,009. * Number of labels: 27 + Neutral. * Maximum sequence length in training and evaluation datasets: 30. On top of the raw data, we also include a version filtered based on reter-agreement, which contains a train/test/validation split: * Size of training dataset: 43,410. * Size of test dataset: 5,427. * Size of validation dataset: 5,426. The emotion categories are: _admiration, amusement, anger, annoyance, approval, caring, confusion, curiosity, desire, disappointment, disapproval, disgust, embarrassment, excitement, fear, gratitude, grief, joy, love, nervousness, optimism, pride, realization, relief, remorse, sadness, surprise_. This directory includes the data and code for data analysis scripts. We also include code for our baseline model, which involves fine-tuning a pre-trained [BERT-base model](https://github.com/google-research/bert). For more details on the design and content of the dataset, please see our [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.00547). Refer to our [GoEmotions Model Card](goemotions_model_card.pdf) for recommended uses of models built with this data, as well as considerations and limitations relating to the GoEmotions data. ## Requirements See `requirements.txt` ## Setup Download the pre-trained BERT model from [here](https://github.com/google-research/bert) and unzip them inside the `bert` directory. In the paper, we use the cased base model. ## Data Our raw dataset can be retrieved by running: ``` wget -P data/full_dataset/ https://storage.googleapis.com/gresearch/goemotions/data/full_dataset/goemotions_1.csv wget -P data/full_dataset/ https://storage.googleapis.com/gresearch/goemotions/data/full_dataset/goemotions_2.csv wget -P data/full_dataset/ https://storage.googleapis.com/gresearch/goemotions/data/full_dataset/goemotions_3.csv ``` See the `data` folder for more detailed data information. ### Data Format Our raw dataset, split into three csv files, includes all annotations as well as metadata on the comments. Each row represents a single rater's annotation for a single example. This file includes the following columns: * `text`: The text of the comment (with masked tokens, as described in the paper). * `id`: The unique id of the comment. * `author`: The Reddit username of the comment's author. * `subreddit`: The subreddit that the comment belongs to. * `link_id`: The link id of the comment. * `parent_id`: The parent id of the comment. * `created_utc`: The timestamp of the comment. * `rater_id`: The unique id of the annotator. * `example_very_unclear`: Whether the annotator marked the example as being very unclear or difficult to label (in this case they did not choose any emotion labels). * separate columns representing each of the emotion categories, with binary labels (0 or 1) The data we used for training the models includes examples where there is agreement between at least 2 raters. Our data includes 43,410 training examples (`train.tsv`), 5426 dev examples (`dev.tsv`) and 5427 test examples (`test.tsv`). These files have _no header row_ and have the following columns: 1. text 2. comma-separated list of emotion ids (the ids are indexed based on the order of emotions in `emotions.txt`) 3. id of the comment ### Visualization [Here](https://nlp.stanford.edu/~ddemszky/goemotions/tsne.html) you can view a TSNE projection showing a random sample of the data. The plot is generated using PPCA (see scripts below). Each point in the plot represents a single example and the text and the labels are shown on mouse-hover. The color of each point is the weighted average of the RGB values of the those emotions. ## Data Analysis See each script for more documentation and descriptive command line flags. * `python3 -m analyze_data`: get high-level statistics of the data and correlation among emotion ratings. * `python3 -m extract_words`: get the words that are significantly associated with each emotion, in contrast to the other emotions, based on their log odds ratio. * `python3 -m ppca`: run PPCA [(Cowen et al., 2019)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-019-0533-6) on the data and generate plots. ## Training and Evaluating Models Run `python -m bert_classifier` to perform fine-tuning on top of BERT, with added regularization. See the script and the paper for detailed description of the flags and parameters. ### Tutorial We released a [detailed tutorial](https://github.com/tensorflow/models/blob/master/research/seq_flow_lite/demo/colab/emotion_colab.ipynb) for training a neural emotion prediction model. In it, we work through training a model architecture available on TensorFlow Model Garden using GoEmotions and applying it for the task of suggesting emojis based on conversational text. ## Citation If you use this code for your publication, please cite the original paper: ``` @inproceedings{demszky2020goemotions, author = {Demszky, Dorottya and Movshovitz-Attias, Dana and Ko, Jeongwoo and Cowen, Alan and Nemade, Gaurav and Ravi, Sujith}, booktitle = {58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL)}, title = {{GoEmotions: A Dataset of Fine-Grained Emotions}}, year = {2020} } ``` ## Contact [Dora Demszky](https://nlp.stanford.edu/~ddemszky/index.html) ## Disclaimer - We are aware that the dataset contains biases and is not representative of global diversity. - We are aware that the dataset contains potentially problematic content. - Potential biases in the data include: Inherent biases in Reddit and user base biases, the offensive/vulgar word lists used for data filtering, inherent or unconscious bias in assessment of offensive identity labels, annotators were all native English speakers from India. All these likely affect labelling, precision, and recall for a trained model. - The emotion pilot model used for sentiment labeling, was trained on examples reviewed by the research team. - Anyone using this dataset should be aware of these limitations of the dataset. ## Dataset Metadata The following table is necessary for this dataset to be indexed by search engines such as Google Dataset Search.

## :beers: What is it? **BEIR** is a **heterogeneous benchmark** containing diverse IR tasks. It also provides a **common and easy framework** for evaluation of your NLP-based retrieval models within the benchmark. For **an overview**, checkout our **new wiki** page: [https://github.com/beir-cellar/beir/wiki](https://github.com/beir-cellar/beir/wiki). For **models and datasets**, checkout out **Hugging Face (HF)** page: [https://huggingface.co/BeIR](https://huggingface.co/BeIR). For more information, checkout out our publications: - [BEIR: A Heterogenous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models](https://openreview.net/forum?id=wCu6T5xFjeJ) (NeurIPS 2021, Datasets and Benchmarks Track) - [Resources for Brewing BEIR: Reproducible Reference Models and an Official Leaderboard](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3626772.3657862) (SIGIR 2024 Resource Track) ## :beers: Installation Install via pip: ```python pip install beir ``` If you want to build from source, use: ```python $ git clone https://github.com/beir-cellar/beir.git $ cd beir $ pip install -e . ``` Tested with python versions 3.9+ ## :beers: Features - Preprocess your own IR dataset or use one of the already-preprocessed 17 benchmark datasets - Wide settings included, covers diverse benchmarks useful for both academia and industry - Evaluates well-known retrieval architectures (lexical, dense, sparse and reranking-based) - Add and evaluate your own model in a easy framework using different state-of-the-art evaluation metrics ## :beers: Quick Example For other example codes, please refer to our **[Examples and Tutorials](https://github.com/beir-cellar/beir/wiki/Examples-and-tutorials)** Wiki page.
Quick Example with Sentence-BERT ```python from beir import util, LoggingHandler from beir.retrieval import models from beir.datasets.data_loader import GenericDataLoader from beir.retrieval.evaluation import EvaluateRetrieval from beir.retrieval.search.dense import DenseRetrievalExactSearch as DRES import logging import pathlib, os #### Just some code to print debug information to stdout logging.basicConfig(format='%(asctime)s - %(message)s', datefmt='%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S', level=logging.INFO, handlers=[LoggingHandler()]) #### /print debug information to stdout #### Download scifact.zip dataset and unzip the dataset dataset = "scifact" url = f"https://public.ukp.informatik.tu-darmstadt.de/thakur/BEIR/datasets/{dataset}.zip" out_dir = os.path.join(pathlib.Path(__file__).parent.absolute(), "datasets") data_path = util.download_and_unzip(url, out_dir) #### Provide the data_path where scifact has been downloaded and unzipped corpus, queries, qrels = GenericDataLoader(data_folder=data_path).load(split="test") #### Load the SBERT model and retrieve using cosine-similarity model = DRES(models.SentenceBERT("Alibaba-NLP/gte-modernbert-base"), batch_size=16) retriever = EvaluateRetrieval(model, score_function="cos_sim") # or "dot" for dot product results = retriever.retrieve(corpus, queries) #### Evaluate your model with NDCG@k, MAP@K, Recall@K and Precision@K where k = [1,3,5,10,100,1000] ndcg, _map, recall, precision = retriever.evaluate(qrels, results, retriever.k_values) mrr = retriever.evaluate_custom(qrels, results, retriever.k_values, metric="mrr") ### If you want to save your results and runfile (useful for reranking) results_dir = os.path.join(pathlib.Path(__file__).parent.absolute(), "results") os.makedirs(results_dir, exist_ok=True) #### Save the evaluation runfile & results util.save_runfile(os.path.join(results_dir, f"{dataset}.run.trec"), results) util.save_results(os.path.join(results_dir, f"{dataset}.json"), ndcg, _map, recall, precision, mrr) ```

%(message)s', datefmt='%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S', level=logging.INFO, handlers=[LoggingHandler()]) #### /print debug information to stdout #### Download scifact.zip dataset and unzip the dataset dataset = "scifact" url = f"https://public.ukp.informatik.tu-darmstadt.de/thakur/BEIR/datasets/{dataset}.zip" out_dir = os.path.join(pathlib.Path(__file__).parent.absolute(), "datasets") data_path = util.download_and_unzip(url, out_dir) #### Provide the data_path where scifact has been downloaded and unzipped corpus, queries, qrels = GenericDataLoader(data_folder=data_path).load(split="test") #### Load the Huggingface model and retrieve using cosine-similarity query_prompt = "Instruct: Given a question, retrieve relevant documents that best answer the question\nQuery: " model = DRES( models.HuggingFace( model_path="intfloat/e5-mistral-7b-instruct", max_length=512, pooling="eos", append_eos_token=True, normalize=True, prompts={"query": query_prompt, "passage": ""}, attn_implementation="flash_attention_2", torch_dtype="bfloat16" ), batch_size=128, ) retriever = EvaluateRetrieval(model, score_function="cos_sim") # or "dot" for dot product results = retriever.encode_and_retrieve(corpus, queries, encode_output_path="./embeddings/") #### Evaluate your model with NDCG@k, MAP@K, Recall@K and Precision@K where k = [1,3,5,10,100,1000] ndcg, _map, recall, precision = retriever.evaluate(qrels, results, retriever.k_values) mrr = retriever.evaluate_custom(qrels, results, retriever.k_values, metric="mrr") ### If you want to save your results and runfile (useful for reranking) results_dir = os.path.join(pathlib.Path(__file__).parent.absolute(), "results") os.makedirs(results_dir, exist_ok=True) #### Save the evaluation runfile & results util.save_runfile(os.path.join(results_dir, f"{dataset}.run.trec"), results) util.save_results(os.path.join(results_dir, f"{dataset}.json"), ndcg, _map, recall, precision, mrr) ```

%(message)s', datefmt='%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S', level=logging.INFO, handlers=[LoggingHandler()]) #### /print debug information to stdout #### Download scifact.zip dataset and unzip the dataset dataset = "scifact" url = f"https://public.ukp.informatik.tu-darmstadt.de/thakur/BEIR/datasets/{dataset}.zip" out_dir = os.path.join(pathlib.Path(__file__).parent.absolute(), "datasets") data_path = util.download_and_unzip(url, out_dir) #### Provide the data_path where scifact has been downloaded and unzipped corpus, queries, qrels = GenericDataLoader(data_folder=data_path).load(split="test") cohere_api_key = os.getenv("COHERE_API_KEY") #### Load the Cohere API Embed model and retrieve using cosine-similarity model = DRES( apis.CohereEmbedAPI( api_key=cohere_api_key, model_path="embed-v4.0", normalize=True, torch_dtype="float32" ), batch_size=96, ) retriever = EvaluateRetrieval(model, score_function="cos_sim") # or "dot" for dot product results = retriever.encode_and_retrieve(corpus, queries, encode_output_path="./cohere/embeddings/") #### Evaluate your model with NDCG@k, MAP@K, Recall@K and Precision@K where k = [1,3,5,10,100,1000] ndcg, _map, recall, precision = retriever.evaluate(qrels, results, retriever.k_values) mrr = retriever.evaluate_custom(qrels, results, retriever.k_values, metric="mrr") ### If you want to save your results and runfile (useful for reranking) results_dir = os.path.join(pathlib.Path(__file__).parent.absolute(), "results") os.makedirs(results_dir, exist_ok=True) #### Save the evaluation runfile & results util.save_runfile(os.path.join(results_dir, f"{dataset}.run.trec"), results) util.save_results(os.path.join(results_dir, f"{dataset}.json"), ndcg, _map, recall, precision, mrr) ```

## CREMA-D (Crowd-sourced Emotional Multimodal Actors Dataset) ***Notice:*** If cloning from GitHub fails, try cloning from GitLab at our [CREMA-D mirror](https://gitlab.com/cs-cooper-lab/crema-d-mirror) #### Summary CREMA-D is a data set of 7,442 original clips from 91 actors. These clips were from 48 male and 43 female actors between the ages of 20 and 74 coming from a variety of races and ethnicities (African America, Asian, Caucasian, Hispanic, and Unspecified). Actors spoke from a selection of 12 sentences. The sentences were presented using one of six different emotions (Anger, Disgust, Fear, Happy, Neutral and Sad) and four different emotion levels (Low, Medium, High and Unspecified). Participants rated the emotion and emotion levels based on the combined audiovisual presentation, the video alone, and the audio alone. Due to the large number of ratings needed, this effort was crowd-sourced and a total of 2443 participants each rated 90 unique clips, 30 audio, 30 visual, and 30 audio-visual. 95% of the clips have more than 7 ratings. The *description* below specifies the data made availabe in this repository. For a more complete description of how CREMA-D was created use [this link](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4313618/) or the link below to the paper. #### Access If you access the GitHub repository, please fill out [this form](https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdvOR994_Hsx7OkBU3oCzluXcmxw2P1nr-zBxcPgVBNLdD9Eg/viewform?usp=sf_link). That way we can keep a record of the community of CREMA-D users. #### Contact/Questions If you have questions about this data set, please submit a new issue to the repository or contact . #### Storage requirements Note: This repository uses Git Large File Storage, [git-lfs](https://git-lfs.github.com). You will need to install it on top of your git installation in order to get the video and audio files. If you just download the zip file (~24MB zipped, ~163MB unzipped) then all of the video and audio files will just be links to the git-lfs file. For more information [go here](https://git-lfs.github.com). - **zip download:** Downloading the repository as a zip will get you all of the R scripts and csv files as well as stubs for all of the audio and video files. The zipped size is ~24MB, and the unzipped size is ~163MB. - **git clone:** ~7.55GB is required to clone the whole repository. In addition to the R scripts and csv files, there is audio and video from 7442 recordings as flash video, mp3, and wav files as described below. #### Setup The repository is now mirrored on GitLab at [CREMA-D mirror](https://gitlab.com/cs-cooper-lab/crema-d-mirror) Try cloning from their first: ``` git clone https://gitlab.com/cs-cooper-lab/crema-d-mirror.git ``` Otherwise, you can clone from here: ``` git lfs clone https://github.com/CheyneyComputerScience/CREMA-D.git ``` #### This Directory holds files used in the paper: [Cao H, Cooper DG, Keutmann MK, Gur RC, Nenkova A, Verma R. CREMA-D: Crowd-sourced Emotional Multimodal Actors Dataset. IEEE transactions on affective computing. 2014;5(4):377-390. doi:10.1109/TAFFC.2014.2336244.](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4313618/) #### The collection of the videos is described in this paper: [Keutmann, M. K., Moore, S. L., Savitt, A., & Gur, R. C. (2015). Generating an item pool for translational social cognition research: methodology and initial validation. Behavior research methods, 47(1), 228-234.](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24719265) #### License: This Crowd-sourced Emotional Mutimodal Actors Dataset (CREMA-D) is made available under the Open Database License: http://opendatacommons.org/licenses/odbl/1.0/. Any rights in individual contents of the database are licensed under the Database Contents License: http://opendatacommons.org/licenses/dbcl/1.0/ #### Description ##### Text Data Files: 1. SentenceFilenames.csv - list of movie files used in study 2. finishedEmoResponses.csv - the first emotional response with timing. 3. finishedResponses.csv - the final emotional Responses with emotion levels with repeated and practice responses removed, used to tabulate the votes 4. finisedResponsesWithRepeatWithPractice.csv - the final emotional responses with emotion levels with repeated and practice responses in tact. Used to observe repeated responses and practice responses. 5. processedResults/tabulatedVotes.csv - the tabulated votes for each movie file. 6. VideoDemographics.csv - a mapping of ActorID (the first 4 digits of each video file) to Age, Sex, Race, and Ethicity. ##### R Scripts 1. processFinishedResponses.R - converts the finisedResponses.csv to the tabulated 2. readTabulatedVotes.R - reads processedResults/tabulatedVotes.csv ##### Finished Responses Columns
(finishedResponses.csv and
finishedResponsesWithRepeatWithPractice.csv) - "localid" - a participant identifier - "pos" - the original log file order for the participant - "ans" - the emotion character with level separated by an underscore - "ttr" - the response time in milliseconds - "queryType" - a numeric value specifying the type of stimulus: 1. - voice only, 2. face only, 3. audio-visual - "numTries" - number of extra emotion clicks. - "clipNum" - the file order of the clip from SentenceFilenames.csv - "questNum" - the order of questions for the query type - "subType" - the type of response in the logs, all values are 4 for the final emotion response - "clipName" - the name of the video file - "sessionNums" - the distinct number for the session - "respEmo" - the emotion response - "respLevel" - the emotion level response - "dispEmo" - the displayed emotion - "dispVal" - the displayed value - "dispLevel" - a numeric representation of the displayed value, 20 for low, 50 for med, 80 for hi. ##### Finished EmoResponses Columns
(finishedEmoResponses.csv) - "localid" - a participant identifier - "sessionNums" - the distinct number for the session - "queryType" - a numeric value specifying the type of stimulus: 1. - voice only, 2. face only, 3. audio-visual - "questNum" - the order of questions for the query type - "pos" - the original log file order for the participant - "ttr" - the response time in milliseconds - "numTries" - number of extra emotion clicks. - "clipNum" - the file order of the clip from SentenceFilenames.csv - "clipName" - the name of the video file ##### Summary Table Columns
processedResults/summaryTable.csv - "fileName" - name of the movie file rated - "VoiceVote" - the emotion (or emotions separated by a colon) with the majority vote for Voice ratings. (A, D, F, H, N, or S) - "VoiceLevel" - the numeric rating (or ratings separated by a colon) corresponding to the emotion(s) listed in "VoiceVote" - "FaceVote" - the emotion (or emotions separated by a colon) with the majority vote for Face ratings. (A, D, F, H, N, or S) - "FaceLevel" - the numeric rating (or ratings separated by a colon) corresponding to the emotion(s) listed in "FaceVote" - "MultiModalVote" - the emotion (or emotions separated by a colon) with the majority vote for MultiModal ratings. (A, D, F, H, N, or S) - "MultiModalLevel" - the numeric rating (or ratings separated by a colon) corresponding to the emotion(s) listed in "MultiModalVote" ##### Tabulated Votes Columns
processedResults/tabulatedVotes.csv - "A" - count of Anger Responses - "D" - count of Disgust Responses - "F" - count of Fear Responses - "H" - count of Happy Responses - "N" - count of Neutral Responses - "S" - count of Sad Responses - "fileName" - name of the movie file rated - "numResponses" - total number of responses - "agreement" - proportion of agreement - "emoVote" - the majority vote agreement - "meanEmoResp" - the mean of all emotion levels - "meanAngerResp" - the mean of the anger levels - "meanDisgustResp" - the mean of the disgust levels - "meanFearResp" - the mean of the fear levels - "meanHappyResp" - the mean of the happy levels - "meanNeutralResp" - the mean of the neutral levels - "meanSadResp" - the mean of the sad levels - "medianEmoResp" - the median of all emotion levels - "meanEmoRespNorm" - the normalized mean of all emotion levels - "meanAngerRespNorm" - the normalized mean of anger emotion levels - "meanDisgustRespNorm" - the normalized mean of disgust emotion levels - "meanFearRespNorm" - the normalized mean of fear emotion levels - "meanHappyRespNorm" - the normalized mean of happy emotion levels - "meanNeutralRespNorm" - the normalized mean of neutral emotion levels - "meanSadRespNorm" - the normalized mean of sad emotion levels - "medianEmoRespNorm" - the normalized median of all emotion levels ##### Video Demographics Columns
VideoDemographics.csv - "ActorID" - the first 4 digits of the video/audio file that identifies the actor in the video. - "Age" - the age in years of the actor at the time of the recording - "Sex" - the binary sex that the actor identified - "Race" - African American, Asian, Caucasian, or Unknown - "Ethnicity" - Hispanic or Not Hispanic ##### Filename labeling conventions The Actor id is a 4 digit number at the start of the file. Each subsequent identifier is separated by an underscore (_). Actors spoke from a selection of 12 sentences (in parentheses is the three letter acronym used in the second part of the filename): - It's eleven o'clock (IEO). - That is exactly what happened (TIE). - I'm on my way to the meeting (IOM). - I wonder what this is about (IWW). - The airplane is almost full (TAI). - Maybe tomorrow it will be cold (MTI). - I would like a new alarm clock (IWL) - I think I have a doctor's appointment (ITH). - Don't forget a jacket (DFA). - I think I've seen this before (ITS). - The surface is slick (TSI). - We'll stop in a couple of minutes (WSI). ## About SKAB [![Maintenance](https://img.shields.io/badge/Maintained%3F-yes-green.svg)](https://github.com/waico/SKAB/graphs/commit-activity) [![DOI](https://img.shields.io/badge/DOI-10.34740/kaggle/dsv/1693952-blue.svg)](https://doi.org/10.34740/KAGGLE/DSV/1693952) [![License: GPL v3.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-GPL%20v3.0-green.svg)](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-3.0.html)

We propose the [Skoltech](https://www.skoltech.ru/en) Anomaly Benchmark (SKAB) designed for evaluating the anomaly detection core. SKAB allows working with two main problems (there are two markups for anomalies):

1. Outlier detection (anomalies considered and marked up as single-point anomalies)
2. Changepoint detection (anomalies considered and marked up as collective anomalies)

SKAB consists of the following artifacts:

1. [Datasets](#datasets)
2. [Proposed Leaderboard](#proposed-leaderboard) for outlier detection and changepoint detection problems
3. Python modules for algorithms’ evaluation (now evaluation modules are being imported from [TSAD](https://github.com/waico/tsad) framework, while the details regarding the evaluation process are presented [here](https://github.com/waico/tsad/blob/main/examples/Evaluating.ipynb))
4. Python [core](core/) with algorithms’ implementation
5. Python [notebooks](#notebooks) with anomaly detection pipeline implementation for various algorithms

All the details about SKAB are presented in the following artifacts:

- Position paper (*currently submitted for publication*)
- Talk about the project: [English](https://youtu.be/hjzuKeNYUho) version and [Russian](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VLmmYGc4v2c) version
- Slides about the project: [English](https://drive.google.com/open?id=1dHUevwPp6ftQCEKnRgB4KMp9oLBMSiDM) version and [Russian](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1gThPCNbEaIxhENLm-WTFGO_9PU1Wdwjq/view?usp=share_link) version

## Datasets

The SKAB v0.9 corpus contains 35 individual data files in .csv format (datasets). The [data](data/) folder contains datasets from the benchmark. The structure of the data folder is presented in the [structure](./data/README.md) file. Each dataset represents a single experiment and contains a single anomaly. The datasets represent a multivariate time series collected from the sensors installed on the testbed. Columns in each data file are following:

- `datetime` - Represents dates and times of the moment when the value is written to the database (YYYY-MM-DD hh:mm:ss)
- `Accelerometer1RMS` - Shows a vibration acceleration (Amount of g units)
- `Accelerometer2RMS` - Shows a vibration acceleration (Amount of g units)
- `Current` - Shows the amperage on the electric motor (Ampere)
- `Pressure` - Represents the pressure in the loop after the water pump (Bar)
- `Temperature` - Shows the temperature of the engine body (The degree Celsius)
- `Thermocouple` - Represents the temperature of the fluid in the circulation loop (The degree Celsius)
- `Voltage` - Shows the voltage on the electric motor (Volt)
- `RateRMS` - Represents the circulation flow rate of the fluid inside the loop (Liter per minute)
- `anomaly` - Shows if the point is anomalous (0 or 1)
- `changepoint` - Shows if the point is a changepoint for collective anomalies (0 or 1)

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) for SKAB is presented [here (tbd)]. Russian version of EDA is available on [kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/newintown/eda-example).

ℹ️We have also made a *SKAB teaser* that is a small dataset collected separately but from the same testbed. SKAB teaser is made just for learning/teaching purposes and contains only 4 collective anomalies. All the information is available on [kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/yuriykatser/skoltech-anomaly-benchmark-skab-teaser).

## Proposed Leaderboard

This leaderboard shows performance of algorithms on test set, unlike leaderboard for SKAB v0.9 which evaluates both training and testing data all together. Moreover, the evaluated window of change points is to the right side of actual change point occurence which is in accordance with fact, that it should be impossible to capture event before it occurs. Lastly, the window size for the NAB detection algorithm is set to 60 seconds to reflect the dynamics of the transition as presented in the slides to enable detection of the start of the transition phase which is also marked as change-point.

You can present and evaluate your algorithm using SKAB on [kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/yuriykatser/skoltech-anomaly-benchmark-skab). Leaderboards are also available at paperswithcode.com: [CPD problem](https://paperswithcode.com/sota/change-point-detection-on-skab).

Information about the metrics for anomaly detection and intuition behind the metrics selection can be found in [this](https://medium.com/@katser/a-review-of-anomaly-detection-metrics-with-a-lot-of-related-information-736d88774712) medium article.

## Notebooks

The [notebooks](notebooks/) folder contains jupyter notebooks with the code for the proposed leaderboard results reproducing. We have calculated the results for following commonly known anomaly detection algorithms:

- Isolation forest - *Outlier detection algorithm based on Random forest concept*
- Vanilla LSTM - *NN with LSTM layer*
- Vanilla AE - *Feed-Forward Autoencoder*
- LSTM-AE - *LSTM Autoencoder*
- LSTM-VAE - *LSTM Variational Autoencoder*
- Conv-AE - *Convolutional Autoencoder*
- MSCRED - *Multi-Scale Convolutional Recurrent Encoder-Decoder*
- MSET - *Multivariate State Estimation Technique*

Additionally on the leaderboard were shown the externally calculated results of the following algorithms:

- [ArimaFD](https://github.com/waico/arimafd) - *ARIMA-based fault detection algorithm*
- [T-squared](http://github.com/YKatser/ControlCharts/tree/main/examples) - *Hotelling's T-squared statistics*
- [T-squared+Q (PCA-based)](http://github.com/YKatser/ControlCharts/tree/main/examples) - *Hotelling's T-squared statistics + Q statistics based on PCA*
- [ruptures](https://github.com/deepcharles/ruptures) - *Changepoint detection (CPD) algorithms from ruptures package*
- [CPDE](https://github.com/YKatser/CPDE) - *Ruptures-based changepoint detection ensemble (CPDE) algorithms*

Details regarding the algorithms, including short description, references to scientific papers and code of the initial implementation is available in [this readme](https://github.com/waico/SKAB/tree/master/notebooks#anomaly-detection-algorithms).

## Installation

1. install Python 3.10+ (tested on 3.10.13)

1. install [poetry](https://python-poetry.org/docs/) package manager
   - `brew install poetry`
   > Poetry installs dependencies and locks versions for deterministic installs. Poetry uses [Python's built-in `venv` module](https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html) to create virtual environments. It also uses PEP [517](https://peps.python.org/pep-0517) & [518](https://peps.python.org/pep-0518) specifications to build packages without requiring `setup.py` or `requirements.txt` files.

1. LightGBM base install
   - `brew install lightgbm`

1. install SKAB dependencies, see [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml) for details
   - `poetry install`

1. confirm installation
   - `poetry show --tree` - shows all dependencies installed
   - `poetry env info` - displays information about the current environment (Python version, path, etc)
   - `poetry list` - lists all cli commands

candidates.title: Small document regions under combined scan and layout shifts
candidates.problem: Small captions, footnotes and page numbers can disappear from a layout detector's output when documents are degraded. This can leave a digitisation pipeline with confident but incomplete page structure. Existing robustness and layout-evaluation papers establish the general failure; the proposed interaction study is still an inferred opportunity.
candidates.gap: Study whether training for combined degradations preserves small-region recall and calibrated detection confidence on document genres excluded from training. Robust layout detection and corruption benchmarks already exist; another generic robustness benchmark is insufficient.
candidates.question: Can size-aware consistency learning reduce small-region omissions under compound scan corruption and held-out document genres without increasing false detections?
candidates.hypothesis: Size-aware consistency will help small regions more than ordinary augmentation at matched resolution. Rival explanation: any gain comes from higher resolution or additional training images rather than the objective.

candidates.approach: Use one small detector with a generic-image pretrained backbone. Compare size-aware feature consistency, learned region-level uncertainty and a bounded multi-scale sampling policy. Keep pixel budgets and corruption exposure matched. Do not use DocLayNet-fine-tuned checkpoints when claiming an unseen-genre test.

COCO boxes; document name, collection, category and page number support document-grouped splits. Corruptions are simulated, not real scan histories.
Official 28 GiB core ZIP and Hugging Face route; CDLA-Permissive 1.0. README examples inspected; image archive not downloaded.
5,000–10,000 source pages, one held-out genre, compact detector; reduce to three layout classes if needed, with a narrower claim.
One occasional 8–12 GB GPU; 16 GB host RAM; 40–80 GB storage. Timing, decoding and peak VRAM unmeasured.
Local page overlay showing regions, small-region warnings and confidence; no claim to complete document understanding.

evaluation: Primary metric
Small-region AP averaged over predeclared compound corruptions and held-out genres; define small-area bins on training data.
Split
Group by document and collection before augmentation; reserve a whole genre; source-only validation and confidence fitting. Never place versions of one page in different splits.
Baselines and code
Faster R-CNN and a compact RT-DETR ([official code](https://github.com/lyuwenyu/RT-DETR)); RoDLA and DocLayout-YOLO as methodological references. Retrain on permitted source documents.
Ablations
Size weighting, confidence head and sampling policy separately; also compare single versus combined corruptions at fixed severity and pixel budget.
Uncertainty and errors

Three development seeds, five headline seeds; document-cluster bootstrap; omission/duplication errors by class, box area, genre and severity. Report overall mAP and calibration beside the primary metric.
Useful result without winning
Find corruption combinations where a higher overall mAP hides more missing footnotes or captions.
Interpretation limit
Synthetic scan corruption supports controlled robustness claims, not production OCR completeness or accessibility benefits.

candidates.title: Land-cover confidence when optical quality and sensor availability change
candidates.problem: Optical cloud contamination can make a fused radar–optical classifier over-rely on the poorer input. A 2026 reliability-aware fusion paper already studies this, including a spatial holdout; neither reliability gating nor geographic testing is a new gap.
candidates.gap: The narrower candidate is availability-conditioned uncertainty calibration under combinations of missing modalities and quality changes not used for calibration. Whether this adds enough beyond current fusion and incomplete-multimodal learning is unresolved.
candidates.question: Can availability-conditioned calibration preserve useful land-cover confidence at a fixed review budget when both input availability and corruption type change on held-out regions?
candidates.hypothesis: Conditioning calibration on observed modality availability will reduce worst-regime selective error. Rival explanation: gains are just the benefit of using the SAR-only classifier in difficult cases.

candidates.title: Small road-damage detection across countries and annotation variation
candidates.problem: Road-image detectors lose accuracy across countries and camera conditions. Recent multi-source adaptation and domain-generalisation models already address this transfer problem; aggregate improvements may still hide small-crack misses and sensitivity to box annotation choices.
candidates.gap: Investigate annotation-tolerant training and source-only reliability under a held-out-country protocol. Real annotation noise is not established by RDD2022; controlled box perturbations must be described as simulations.
candidates.question: Can annotation-tolerant assignment and small-damage training preserve held-out-country recall without relying on target-country labels or adaptation?
candidates.hypothesis: A size-aware, box-tolerant objective will improve small-damage recall beyond multi-source empirical risk minimisation. Rival explanation: benefits arise from higher image resolution, country balance or duplicate road frames.

Leave one country out; reserve another source grouping for selection. Remove exact/perceptual duplicates across partitions; keep identifiable capture sequences grouped. Unknown route IDs limit route-level claims.
Baselines and code

Faster R-CNN, compact [YOLO11](https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics), multi-source training and MAMDG/MSDA-RDD as nearest methods. Do not use an RDD-trained checkpoint on a claimed held-out country.
Ablations
Box tolerance, small-region term and calibration; match country weighting, resolution, optimiser and generic pretraining.
Uncertainty and errors
Multiple training seeds; image/capture-group bootstrap within each country; report country results individually because four countries are too few for precise geographic population inference.
Useful result without winning
Show whether small-crack performance is driven more by resolution, source selection or annotation sensitivity than architecture changes.
Interpretation limit
Artificial box perturbations do not prove genuine annotation error. No deployment or automated road-safety benefit follows from benchmark AP.

candidates.title: Preserving search relevance when compact rerankers are quantised
candidates.problem: Quantisation can change which document a search system returns even when ordinary accuracy appears stable. A September 2026 paper demonstrates this for a MiniLM cross-encoder as well as embedding models, so discovering ranking flips is already occupied.
candidates.gap: Investigate training that preserves relevance-bearing pairwise margins under activation-and-weight quantisation and domain transfer. The neighbour explicitly leaves activation quantisation untested and asks whether training can improve useful margins. This supports an opportunity, not certified originality for a particular loss.
candidates.question: Can margin-preserving training reduce relevance loss from an INT8 compact reranker under held-out-domain testing at matched candidate depth and actual latency?
candidates.hypothesis: Quantisation-aware pairwise consistency will preserve judged relevance better than ordinary fine-tuning followed by quantisation. Rival explanation: gains come from the loss/negative pool alone, or INT8 causes negligible damage and needs no special method.

candidates.approach: Keep a BM25 top-100 candidate set fixed. Fine-tune a small cross-encoder with quantisation-aware pairwise consistency, then investigate a bounded full-precision fallback policy. Count both models and fallback calls in memory/latency. Begin with a real INT8 CPU backend; simulated low-bit arithmetic is not evidence of a speedup.
data: Official BEIR ZIP/loading example inspected; dataset cards show roughly 3,633 NFCorpus and 5,183 SciFact documents. Use public query relevance judgments, not model-generated relevance.
BEIR release cards declare CC BY-SA 4.0 for these datasets; framework/model licences are separate. Unjudged documents are not guaranteed irrelevant.
Use NFCorpus training queries and source validation; hold SciFact evaluation queries out of adaptation and calibration. Check query/document duplicates. No new clinical annotations are needed.
Small corpora and CPU INT8 inference; 8–16 GB RAM, under 10 GB disk, occasional 8 GB GPU for fine-tuning. Actual speed, RAM and training time unmeasured.
Top-20 candidates or a frozen encoder plus trained head; state the narrower scope. Local ranked-search demo with relevance and latency comparisons.

Always INT8, always FP, random fallback and fixed thresholds.
Quality–latency frontier including router and FP cost.
evaluation: Primary metric
Held-out-domain nDCG@10 at a predefined measured reranking-latency budget; freeze candidate depth before testing.
Split
Source train/selection/calibration queries disjoint; target-domain judgments used only for final evaluation. Record checkpoint pretraining and exclude target-fine-tuned checkpoints.
Baselines and code

BM25; FP and INT8 [MiniLM-L6-v2](https://huggingface.co/cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2); ordinary QAT, MarginMSE and the published gap-sensitive PTQ idea. Use [Sentence Transformers training code](https://github.com/huggingface/sentence-transformers).
Ablations
Curriculum, paired consistency and routing separately; same teacher, candidate list, negatives, token limits and seeds. Report weight-only versus activation-plus-weight quantisation distinctly.
Uncertainty and errors
Paired query bootstrap and repeated training seeds; latency distributions under fixed threads/batch size with warm-up. Analyse low margins, document length, domain and partial relevance judgments.
Useful result without winning
If INT8 has negligible quality loss or routing costs erase savings, demonstrate when ordinary INT8 is sufficient. FP ranking changes alone do not prove relevance harm.
Interpretation limit
Relevance judgments support retrieval-quality claims, not factual correctness of generated answers or energy savings.

candidates.title: Rare-emotion uncertainty from limited and disagreeing text annotations
candidates.problem: A majority-vote emotion label hides disagreement, especially for rare co-occurring labels. Recent work already models annotator distributions and shows that hard-label calibration and distribution fidelity can move in opposite directions.
candidates.gap: Study finite-vote uncertainty for multi-label emotion probabilities when training annotations are reduced and the source community changes. Marginal probabilities for co-occurring labels must not automatically be forced into a single categorical distribution. Soft-label learning itself is established.
candidates.question: Can vote-count-aware shrinkage and label-dependence learning preserve rare-label probability quality under reduced annotation budgets and held-out Reddit communities?
candidates.hypothesis: Accounting for the finite number of votes will reduce rare-label overconfidence without erasing minority labels. Rival explanation: simple class balancing or ordinary soft-label BCE explains the entire gain.

candidates.approach: Cache a generic frozen text encoder's features. Train vote-count-aware probabilistic heads and a small dependency model. Fit calibration on source-only validation communities. Evaluate each label as a Bernoulli marginal; only use a normalised distribution metric when the label representation genuinely warrants it.
data: Use raw per-rater CSVs, with comment, rater, author, thread and subreddit fields. The agreement-filtered 43,410/5,426/5,427 split is insufficient on its own for raw disagreement analysis.
Original Google Storage loading commands and schema inspected; official dataset card declares Apache 2.0. Public release card is 28.3 MB across configurations, not a measured raw-CSV footprint.
Group comments by thread and author; hold out subreddits. Finite votes estimate annotator-population marginals, not a person's hidden emotion. No new annotation is required.
Frozen encoder plus small heads: 4–8 GB RAM, under 5 GB disk; one-off CPU or modest-GPU embedding extraction. Runtime unmeasured.
Common-label subset with the reduced scope stated; local text probabilities and uncertainty display. Do not use a checkpoint already tuned on held-out GoEmotions comments.

Soft BCE; remove count/shrinkage terms.
Marginal Brier score versus number of votes.
B: co-occurrence
Does a learned dependence term help rare joint labels?
Train a small structured dependency component.
Independent heads; remove dependency edges.
Rare/co-occurring label recall and probability error.
C: transfer calibration
Can source-only pooling improve community-held-out confidence?
Fit partially pooled label/group calibrators.
Global temperature/vector scaling; remove pooling.
Worst-community calibration and selective risk.
evaluation: Primary metric
Macro-average marginal Brier score against full held-out per-rater vote proportions; report rare-label strata and vote-count uncertainty.
Split
All votes for one comment stay together; group by thread and author, and hold out communities. Fit encoders/heads/calibrators only on permitted source partitions.
Baselines and code

TF–IDF logistic regression, the [original BERT baseline](https://github.com/google-research/google-research/blob/master/goemotions/bert_classifier.py), frozen RoBERTa soft-BCE heads and cSG-MCMC-head reimplementation from its paper; exact cSG-MCMC checkpoint availability unverified.
Ablations
Finite-vote shrinkage, dependency term and calibration pooling; hold model, annotation count and class weighting fixed. Simulate reduced training votes without reducing the full test reference.
Uncertainty and errors
Training seeds plus nested comment/thread and rater resampling where assignments support it. Stratify by label frequency, co-occurrence, vote count and community.
Useful result without winning
Find where aggregate accuracy or a categorical normalisation hides poor marginal probabilities for rare co-occurring emotions.
Interpretation limit
A few votes cannot identify a precise universal emotion distribution. Existing social-media labels do not validate mental-state, hiring or clinical inference.

candidates.title: Recovering short, low-consensus sound events from soft labels
candidates.problem: Low-consensus sounds can disappear when soft labels are thresholded, and temporal smoothing can suppress short events. Existing MAESTRO work already demonstrates benefits from soft labels and rare-event detection; those benefits are not a new contribution.
candidates.gap: Investigate duration-aware training and pooling for low-consensus event segments, with explicit handling of classes not annotated in a scene. The release only resolves one-second segments, so it cannot validate sub-second onset precision.
candidates.question: Can duration-aware soft-target learning improve one-to-three-second event detection without trading away probability fidelity or increasing false alarms on annotated negative segments?
candidates.hypothesis: A duration-aware objective will reduce short-event suppression beyond ordinary soft BCE at matched backbone size. Rival explanation: apparent gains are just lower thresholds, altered smoothing or treating unannotated classes as negatives.

Use only documented eligible class/scene labels; never turn an unavailable annotation into a negative.

README duration/class listing does not fully match inspected annotations. One soft value lies outside [0,1] beyond roundoff; locate it and predeclare exclusion/clipping sensitivity before training.

Development audio listed as 2,614,126,654 bytes; custom experimental/non-commercial licence. The separate evaluation release must supply labels before it can be used locally; otherwise use grouped development folds.
CPU feature preparation plus occasional modest GPU; 8–16 GB RAM and 8–20 GB disk. A frozen audio-embedding head is the fallback; no runtime measured.
Local sound timeline at one-second resolution. No claim to detect physical hazards or give precise event onsets.

evaluation: Primary metric
Macro soft Brier score on eligible one-second class/segments; predeclare short-event recall as the key secondary outcome rather than inventing sub-second ground truth.
Split
Group all segments from an original recording and location/capture together. Use development folds for fitting/selection; no evaluation-waveform adaptation.
Baselines and code

Published CRNN hard-BCE, soft-BCE and soft-MSE models; compact CRNN with [DCASE evaluation tools](https://github.com/fgnt/sed_scores_eval); Dual-Conformer is a stronger reference whose exact training/checkpoints remain unverified.
Ablations
Duration loss, pooling and calibration; fixed time resolution, data, class eligibility and smoothing. Report missing-label masks separately from negative labels.
Uncertainty and errors
Recording-cluster bootstrap and repeated seeds; analyse event duration, polyphony, soft-consensus level and class. Report interval instability for rare classes.
Useful result without winning
Show whether short-event gains are just threshold/smoothing changes or whether probability fidelity worsens while hard F1 improves.
Interpretation limit
Annotation-derived duration is one-second resolution. Soft values represent aggregated opinions, not physical event probabilities.

candidates.title: Audio emotion confidence with modality-matched annotations
candidates.problem: The same acted utterance receives different audio-only and audiovisual emotion judgments. Supervising an audio-only model with a pooled or audiovisual target can therefore train it toward information absent from its input. Generic annotator disagreement and cross-corpus uncertainty are already studied.
candidates.gap: Investigate modality-matched probability targets and controlled transfer of information from paired annotation views, evaluated against existing audio-only votes on unseen actors. This is a listener-judgment modelling problem, not inference of a speaker's true mental state.
candidates.question: Can modality-aware soft-target learning reduce an audio-only classifier's overconfidence relative to held-out audio-only ratings without requiring new annotations?
candidates.hypothesis: Modality-matched targets plus a constrained cross-view regulariser will improve audio-only vote fidelity. Rival explanation: any apparent gain comes from speaker or sentence leakage, or ordinary soft-label training.

Frozen features and small heads: 8 GB RAM, 10–20 GB disk; optional modest GPU for extraction/fine-tuning. Validate media access and known damaged files before training.
Restrict to verified actors and recordings, preserving actor holdouts; local audio-only vote-probability display. No claims about clinical, workplace or hidden emotional states.

Brier score against existing audio-only vote proportions; use per-clip count-aware uncertainty and distribution distance as secondary outcomes.
Split
Actor-disjoint train/validation/test; additional sentence-held-out diagnostic. All views and encodings of a clip stay together; actor IDs are grouping variables, never input features.
Baselines and code

MFCC/openSMILE-style features with logistic regression; frozen wav2vec2/audio embeddings plus MLP; soft-label/dropout and the 2024 uncertainty methods. [SpeechBrain](https://github.com/speechbrain/speechbrain) is an implementation route, not proof of a matching pretrained split.
Ablations
Target view, count model, constrained view transfer and calibration independently; identical encoder/features and rater counts.
Uncertainty and errors
Actor-cluster bootstrap, rater resampling where assignments permit and training seeds; errors by sentence, intended class and cross-view disagreement.
Useful result without winning
Demonstrate when intended labels or audiovisual votes give deceptively confident scores for an audio-only model.
Interpretation limit
A codec/noise transformation has no new human ratings here; do not claim its perceived-emotion uncertainty is ground-truthed by clean-audio votes. No new participant study is assumed.

candidates.title: Choosing anomaly detectors when sensor availability changes
candidates.area: Time series / anomaly detection / model selection
candidates.problem: A detector that ranks well on one sensor stream need not be the best on another, and current unsupervised selectors can be far from an oracle. Missing channels can also alter reconstruction scores and alarm rates. The proposed selector's response to missing channels remains a hypothesis, not an already measured failure here.
candidates.gap: Learn context-dependent detector selection or ensemble weights under changed sensor availability, while locking alarm calibration without test anomaly labels. Neither model selection nor low-false-alarm evaluation alone is new.
candidates.question: Can a selector trained on normal data and controlled proxy faults choose more useful detectors under sensor dropout than a fixed detector or static selector at the same false-alarm budget?
candidates.hypothesis: Availability-aware proxy evaluation will reduce detector-selection regret after channels disappear. Rival explanation: a fixed robust detector or a simple median ensemble explains all gains, and synthetic proxy faults mis-rank real faults.

candidates.approach: Build a pool of four or five small detectors. Generate proxy corruptions only from normal training data, fit a regularised selector, and investigate availability-conditioned ensemble weighting. Real test anomaly labels are reserved for the evaluator and an explicitly labelled oracle bound.
data: [SKAB author release](https://github.com/waico/SKAB): 34 anomaly experiments plus a normal-only file, eight sensor channels, anomaly/changepoint labels.
Original README, data-folder schema and first rows of valve1/1.csv inspected through GitHub. Columns confirm timestamps, sensors and two label fields.
Repository release is GPL-3.0; retain its terms when using/distributing code or data. One physical testbed and few independent faults limit claims about general industrial monitoring.
Reserve whole experiments/fault groups before windows; fit normalisation and thresholds on normal training/calibration blocks. Repeated masks from one experiment are not independent test cases.
CPU-first small models, 8 GB RAM and under 5 GB working data. Small TCN/GRU training can use occasional GPU; wall time and full data footprint unmeasured.
Three detectors and one dropout family; retain independent experiment holdouts. Offline alarm timeline with selected model and false-alarm counts.

Recall–false-alarm trade-offs and weight stability.
evaluation: Primary metric
Event recall at a predeclared calibration false-alarm budget; report realised false-alarm events per normal hour on test separately, without retuning.
Split
Whole experiments and fault families disjoint; causal windows, no point adjustment, no test-label threshold selection and no labelled test anomalies in selector fitting.
Baselines and code

PCA/Isolation Forest, causal TCN and GRU autoencoder; fixed best-source detector, random/static selection and median ensemble. [mTSBench code](https://github.com/PLAN-Lab/mTSBench) supplies modern selector references; reproduce their prerequisites or label an omission.
Ablations
Proxy weighting, availability features and ensemble constraints; match detector pool, missing-data treatment and calibration access.
Uncertainty and errors
Experiment-cluster bootstrap plus detector/selector seeds; report each fault family, dropout pattern, detection delay and missed events. Use raw scores and label access logs.
Useful result without winning
Identify when proxy faults give misleading rankings, or when a single robust detector beats a complex selector.
Interpretation limit
A single testbed cannot validate general industrial reliability. Fixed calibration thresholds do not guarantee future false-alarm control under shift.

candidates.title: Activity transitions under unfamiliar sensor sampling patterns
candidates.problem: Sampling patterns can become predictive shortcuts, while sparse or irregular observations obscure brief activity transitions. Recent PRISM and SIGHT papers document sampling-shift and temporal-adaptation limitations. Generic sampling-rate robustness and adversarial augmentation already exist.
candidates.gap: Study constrained learned sampling augmentation together with transition-sensitive temporal learning, tested under coupled observation and signal shifts. PRISM explicitly leaves learned plausible sampling generators and coupled feature shifts open; this does not prove that a particular generator is novel.
candidates.question: Can a source-trained, constrained sampling curriculum preserve postural-transition recognition under unseen dropout/rate patterns better than fixed sampling augmentation?
candidates.hypothesis: A budget-constrained adversarial sampling policy will improve transition recall without exploiting class-dependent missingness shortcuts. Rival explanation: fixed downsampling augmentation or a larger receptive field suffices.

candidates.approach: Train a small time-aware temporal model and a constrained mask/rate curriculum on source subjects. Add a transition-sensitive objective and source-only calibration. Keep mask families class-balanced and hold out sampling patterns. The regular original data does not provide measured real dropout mechanisms; generated masks are controlled tests.
data: Thirty subjects, 50 Hz acceleration/gyroscope raw streams, six activities and six postural transitions. RawData/labels.txt supplies experiment, user, activity and start/end sample indices.
Official direct ZIP route listed as 75.9 MB; CC BY 4.0. File list and loading documentation inspected; raw archive not downloaded.
Use raw sequences and transition labels, not only pre-windowed 561-feature records. Partition subjects and whole recordings before resampling/windowing.
CPU-first small CNN/GRU/TCN, 4–8 GB RAM and under 5 GB working disk; optional modest GPU. Original-to-generated size expansion must be capped.
Fixed augmentation plus a learned small policy on fewer mask families; local activity replay. No continuous wearable deployment or medical claims.

Selective risk by transition and sampling condition.
evaluation: Primary metric
Subject-macro transition F1, with transition definitions/tolerances frozen from training and validation; include ordinary-activity macro-F1.
Split
Subject-disjoint raw recordings; hold out sampling-pattern families. Keep overlapping windows and all resampled versions of a recording together; no target-subject labels for tuning.
Baselines and code

Handcrafted features/SVM, DeepConvLSTM or small TCN, fixed sampling augmentation, PRISM and SIGHT as modern references. [ViTST code](https://github.com/Leezekun/ViTST) provides an additional irregular-series baseline; exact PRISM anonymous-code access remains unverified.
Ablations
Learned policy, transition loss and calibration; also compare sampling-only, feature-only and coupled shifts at matched observed samples.
Uncertainty and errors
Subject-cluster bootstrap, repeated training/mask seeds; errors by transition, remaining sampling density, burst length and channel loss.
Useful result without winning
Show when dropout augmentation creates label shortcuts or when apparent robustness hides missed transitions.
Interpretation limit
The waist-mounted laboratory protocol does not establish cross-device, clinical or real dropout-process generalisation. Do not invent physical energy savings from dropped samples.

candidates.title: Intermittent-demand intervals that distinguish missing readings from zero sales
candidates.problem: Missing observations and genuine zero sales have different meanings for intermittent-demand forecasts. The Monash Car Parts archive releases both original missing values and a zero-filled variant, making their effects directly testable without collecting new business data.
candidates.gap: Investigate missingness-aware occurrence/size modelling and pooled uncertainty after long observed zero runs. Probabilistic forecast combinations and zero-preserving feature engineering already exist; simply correcting preprocessing is insufficient for three research contributions.
candidates.question: Can a missingness-aware occurrence/size model with history-conditioned pooling improve prediction intervals for intermittent demand without treating unobserved sales as zero?
candidates.hypothesis: Separating observation availability from zero demand will improve probability quality, particularly after long zero runs. Rival explanation: gains are purely a preprocessing correction or ordinary cross-series pooling rather than a new modelling contribution.

candidates.approach: Train a small two-part occurrence/positive-size model with an explicit observation mask. Investigate missingness-aware likelihood/training weights, pooled interval calibration and a learned history-based pooling policy. Treat the two archive variants as an audit comparison, not as independent validation datasets.
data: Monash [original Car Parts](https://zenodo.org/records/4656022) and [zero-filled variant](https://zenodo.org/records/4656021). Both API records and CC BY 4.0 licences checked.
The 39,656-byte original ZIP contains 2,674 monthly series of length 51, with 6,122 missing markers and 97,398 observed zero entries. Counts and archive hash are in the metadata audit.
Observed sales are the targets. No inventory, stockout, price or part-family metadata is assumed; do not infer unmet demand or obsolescence causes from zeros.
Rolling origins; select models, calibration history and zero-run strata using only past observations. Exclude genuinely missing evaluation targets rather than calling imputations ground truth.
CPU boosting or a small global hurdle model, 2–8 GB RAM and under 2 GB disk. The source parsing is demonstrated; training time and model memory are unmeasured.
Fewer series and shorter forecast horizons, retaining the original missingness flags; local intermittent-sales replay with intervals and observation availability.

Train occurrence/positive-size heads with missingness-aware likelihood or weights.
Same clean preprocessing with ordinary hurdle/quantile model; remove mask-aware term.
Probability/quantile error by zero-run length.
B: interval updates
Can pooled calibration protect low-history series?
Fit history-conditioned partially pooled interval calibration.
Global and per-series rolling calibration; remove pooling.
Coverage/width across history and sparsity strata.
C: sharing policy
Can past-only similarity improve sharing without negative transfer?
Learn cross-series grouping or shrinkage weights from training histories.
Uniform/global pooling and static clusters; remove learned policy.
Worst-series trade-offs and negative-transfer cases.
evaluation: Primary metric

Mean scaled weighted interval score over observed test targets, using training-only scaling and a predefined safeguard/report for all-zero training series. Report unscaled interval score as a sensitivity check.
Split

Rolling-origin chronological train/selection/calibration/test periods. Series-group holdouts only if making a new-series claim; the core forecasts known series. Both archive variants use identical observed target indices.
Baselines and code

Zero/seasonal-naive, Croston/SBA/TSB, zero-inflated or hurdle model, quantile LightGBM and scoring-rule forecast combinations. [StatsForecast](https://github.com/Nixtla/statsforecast) and the [Monash evaluation repository](https://github.com/rakshitha123/TSForecasting) are implementation routes.
Ablations

Missingness-aware predictive term, interval pooling and learned sharing. Include zero-filled versus original-input variants while scoring only genuinely observed targets; match lags and training examples.
Uncertainty and errors

Series-cluster and time-block resampling, several model seeds; coverage by past zero-run length, historical observation count, horizon and sparsity. Report near-zero interval collapse and nonzero-demand misses.
Useful result without winning
Quantify when zero filling changes conclusions or when a simple occurrence/size model outperforms a more complex temporal model.
Interpretation limit
Only 51 historical months per series and an old domain are available. No causal stockout, inventory-cost, modern retail or operational service-level claim is supported.
